strengths: Novel and clearly stated central contribution: the first demonstration that linear mode connectivity (LMC) can hold between model soup ingredients that differ in their self-supervised training runs — including different SSL objectives (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR), not merely different hyperparameters. This genuinely expands the known cases where souping works (Fig. 2, §4.1).

Careful and fair baseline design: the authors construct a 'continued SSL + supervised soup' baseline with equal search cost (Fig. 3), so gains are not simply attributable to extra compute; supervised soups and TTA (SAR) are also compared (Tab. 3).

Extensive evaluation: ImageNet plus 7 shifted test sets, VTAB across 21 tasks × 16 corruption conditions (336 test sets), disjoint vs. joint splits to quantify the effect of using test-distribution data, and a second stock (Franca) to probe generality (Fig. 4).

The strongest results (+3.5% IN-C, +7% LAION-C) are cleanly attributed: inter-training on the shifted distribution rather than the test samples themselves delivers most of the gain, and the disjoint-split controls make this credible.

Self-Seasoning is a sensible label-free extension of seasoning (kNN-entropy minimization over mixture coefficients) with released PyTorch code (Appendix D), and the paper is honest that supervised seasoning still beats it overall (Tab. 5).

Reproducibility is reasonably strong: hyperparameters, schedules, and implementation details are provided in Appendix B, and the mini-VTAB-C benchmark is shared. The limitations section is candid about modest gains and the need for unlabeled shifted data.
weaknesses: Many headline gains are small: on VTAB the Self-Soup advantage over the continued SSL + supervised soup baseline is ~0.3–1% mean accuracy (Tab. 4), and on ImageNet the IN-Val gain is negative for uniform mixing (79.11 vs 79.23, Tab. 1). No error bars or statistical significance are reported for any comparison, so it is hard to judge robustness of ≲1% differences.

The largest gains (+3.5%, +7%) require unlabeled data from the corrupted test distribution — essentially transductive/domain-adaptation access that will often be unavailable, as the authors themselves concede. The more practically relevant in-distribution gains are much smaller.

Scale and generality are limited: experiments are at ViT-B with mostly one stock (MAE); the second stock (Franca) is tested only with pairwise MAE–MoCoV3 mixes. Fine-tuning is only 10 epochs, and it is unclear whether gains persist with longer or stronger fine-tuning recipes.

Compute cost of the method is discussed only qualitatively. Inter-training multiple models (e.g., 4 × 100K steps on ImageNet-C) plus N fine-tunings per inter-training is expensive; a quantitative cost accounting versus the accuracy gains would strengthen the deployment-cost argument.

The formalization (Eq. 2) is largely notational — the framework is 'any soup whose ingredients differ in SSL runs' — so the paper's methodological contribution rests almost entirely on its empirical findings, and the space of design choices explored (3 SSL algorithms, arbitrary hyperparameters) is acknowledged to be a small slice.

Results are mixed across corruption families (worse on noise by -1%, Tab. 4b), and Self-Seasoning underperforms substantially on several structured tasks (e.g., Clevr-Count 17.5 vs 34.6, dSpr-Loc-X 4.1 vs 11.6), which tempers the claim that label-free mixing is broadly 'competitive.'

strengths: Clear and well-organized presentation; the 'soup kitchen' framing (stock/ingredients/seasoning) is consistent and the figures (Fig. 1-3) do a good job situating Self-Soupervision relative to Model Soups and Model Ratatouille.

The central empirical finding — that linear mode connectivity can hold between ingredients that differ in their self-supervised training runs, including across fundamentally different SSL families (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR) — is genuinely novel and is demonstrated with a fairly thorough mixture-space sweep (52 mixtures across 8 test sets, Fig. 2).

The baselines are thoughtfully constructed: the 'continued SSL + supervised soup' baseline matches the Self-Soup search cost (Fig. 3), so the comparison is fair in terms of development budget, and the paper correctly identifies when soups are worth the extra search cost.

Honest limitations discussion: the paper acknowledges that the largest gains (+7% LAION-C) require unlabeled target/shifted data, that other gains are modest (≲1%), and that only 3 SSL families are covered.
Considerable hyperparameter and training detail in Appendix B, and the bonus TTA experiment (Tab. 3) showing Self-Soups and SAR are complementary adds value.
weaknesses: The headline gains are much smaller than the abstract suggests: on standard (non-transductive) settings the improvements over appropriately matched baselines are typically ≲1% (e.g., Table 1: Uniform Mix 32.23 vs 31.24 on IN-C; 79.11 vs 79.23 on IN-Val, i.e., slightly worse). The +3.5%/+7% claims only hold when inter-training on the test distribution, which is a transductive/test-time-training-style setting with limited applicability and is only partially acknowledged.

No statistical rigor: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere. Given that many claimed gains are within a few tenths of a percent, it is impossible to judge whether the differences between Self-Soups and the continued-SSL baseline are meaningful.

Reproducibility claims are not fulfilled: Appendix C ('Data and Code') is essentially blank — two headings with no content — despite the main text repeatedly promising that mini-VTAB-C and PyTorch code are 'shared in the supplement'. This is a serious gap for a paper whose contribution is primarily empirical.

The VTAB evaluation uses a custom 'mini-VTAB' with 1K-sample train/test subsets, which breaks comparability with the literature and may inflate variance; results are correspondingly mixed (e.g., Table 5: Self-Seasoning is best on only 4/21 tasks and badly underperforms on dSpr-Loc-X, 4.1 vs 11.6).

The transductive experiments lack sufficient baselines: SAR is the only TTA method compared, and there is no comparison against test-time training (TTT) or UDA-style baselines given the same unlabeled shifted data budget, which is the natural competitor for the setting where the big gains occur.

Some experimental choices appear under-justified (SSL hyperparameters 'mostly chosen arbitrarily'; Self-Seasoning optimizer settings 'did not tune this because it worked well enough'), and the number of ingredients is small (3-6), leaving open whether the finding scales.

strengths: Genuinely novel finding: the paper is the first to demonstrate that linear mode connectivity (LMC) holds between ingredients trained with different self-supervised algorithms (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR spanning three SSL families), expanding the known regimes where model soups work. This is a meaningful contribution to the understanding of weight averaging.

Well-designed, fair baselines: the 'continued SSL + supervised soup' baseline matches the search/development cost of Self-Soups (Fig. 3), which is an unusually careful experimental control for the soups literature and strengthens the core claim that self-supervised ingredients themselves add value.

Broad evaluation: 8 ImageNet test sets, VTAB across 21 tasks x 16 corruption/natural conditions (336 test sets), a second stock (Franca), test-time adaptation comparison (SAR), and a disjoint/joint split of test-distribution inter-training to rule out trivial leakage (Tab. 2).

The Self-Seasoning contribution (label-free mixture selection via kNN entropy minimization) is a sensible, well-motivated extension, and the results are honestly reported as 'competitive' rather than oversold relative to label-based seasoning.

Honest limitations section that correctly identifies the modest magnitude of non-shift gains (~1%), the dependence of the largest gains (+7%) on unlabeled shifted data, and the restricted set of SSL families.

Reproducibility of the core experiments is strong: full training details (optimizers, learning rates, masking ratios, decoder settings, LPFT usage) are given in Appendix B, and PyTorch code for Self-Seasoning is included in Appendix D.
weaknesses: Magnitude of gains is small in most settings: roughly +1% on IN-C, +0.4% on LAION-C, and ~+0.5-0.8% averaged over VTAB. The headline +3.5%/+7% gains require inter-training on unlabeled corrupted test-distribution data, a setting whose practical applicability the authors themselves concede may often be unavailable. No statistical significance, error bars, or seed variance is reported for any result, which is concerning given the small margins.

Appendix C ('Data and Code') is essentially empty: the main text states mini-VTAB-C is 'shared in the supplement (§C)' and promises PyTorch code, but the section contains only placeholder headings. This is a reproducibility gap that undermines the otherwise good supplementary detail.

The core souping experiments (§4.1, §4.2) use only M=3 ingredients and 5-epoch inter-training runs; the ingredient-diversity axis is explored thinly, and SSL hyperparameters were 'mostly chosen arbitrarily', leaving open how sensitive the LMC-across-SSL-algorithms finding is to these choices.

Scale and architecture coverage are limited: one backbone family (ViT-B) and only two stocks (MAE and Franca); 'mini-VTAB' uses 1K-sample subsets, which is far from the standard VTAB protocol and makes direct comparison to published VTAB results impossible.

Some results are internally unflattering yet presented positively: in §4.5, Self-Seasoning is the most accurate on only 4/21 tasks and is clearly worse than label-based seasoning on structured datasets (e.g., dSpr-Loc-Y 7.3 vs 17.9), so 'competitive' is a generous characterization; likewise noise robustness is worse than the supervised-only soup (-1%).

The claim of being the 'first' to soup ingredients differing in SSL runs should be more carefully verified against related continued-SSL/weight-averaging work (e.g., Diet-CP, continued pretraining averaging), and the paper would benefit from analysis of *why* LMC holds across different SSL objectives rather than purely empirical demonstration.

Writing relies heavily on the cooking metaphor ('stock', 'seasoning', 'ingredients', 'tasty'), which occasionally obscures rather than clarifies the formal method (Eq. 2 is trivial given the framing).

strengths: Novel and well-motivated extension of the model soup literature to self-supervised ingredients: the demonstration that linear mode connectivity (LMC) holds between ingredients that differ in their SSL algorithm (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR, LeJEPA) and hyperparameters is a genuinely new finding (Fig. 2), with careful visualization of the mixture space.

Extensive and mostly fair experimental design: the authors introduce a 'continued SSL + supervised soup' baseline with equal search budget (Fig. 3) so that gains are attributable to souping across SSL runs rather than extra SSL training; they compare against ensembles, Model Ratatouille, and SOTA test-time adaptation (SAR, Tab. 3), and validate on a second stock (Franca, Fig. 5).

The test-distribution inter-training experiment (§4.3) is carefully controlled with disjoint even/odd-indexed splits, showing the large +3.5%/+7% robustness gains do not require training on test samples themselves.

Self-Seasoning is a sensible unsupervised mixing scheme (kNN-entropy minimization over mixture coefficients, Eq. 3), and the few-shot study (Tab. 9, Fig. 4) with a matched labeled-seasoning control is a nice ablation showing value when labels are scarce.
Honest limitations discussion: the authors acknowledge that the largest gains require unlabeled target/shifted data, that other gains are modest (<1%), and that only 3 SSL families are covered.
weaknesses: Headline gains are somewhat overstated relative to typical results: outside the test-distribution setting, improvements over the strong continued-SSL baseline are consistently small (e.g., +0.9% on IN-C/LAION-C in Tab. 1, +0.5-1.4% on VTAB in Tab. 4), and in some cases negative (e.g., -1% on noise corruptions); no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported to support claims of these differences.

The abstract's '+3.5% (ImageNet-C) and +7% (LAION-C)' numbers come from the setting where unlabeled test-distribution data is assumed available for inter-training—effectively an unsupervised domain adaptation assumption that limits practical applicability; the paper only discloses this in the limitations section.

Reproducibility is undermined: Section D 'Data and Code' is empty in the manuscript, the code URL in the abstract is truncated ('https://github.com/'), and several experiments depend on a non-standard 'mini-VTAB' (1K subsets) whose construction is relegated to the supplement.

Supplementary tables have confusing/erroneous cross-references (Table 6 and Table 7 captions each say 'same experiment setup as Tab. 7'), and main-text results refer to supplemental Tab. 7 for core comparisons, making verification awkward.

Scope is narrow: a single architecture scale (ViT-B), one SSL stock for most experiments, and VTAB experiments on 1K-sample subsets reduce confidence in generalization of the modest gains to practical settings.

Self-Seasoning, while functional, is a fairly incremental technique (entropy minimization on kNN predictions, directly inspired by TTA methods like TENT), and its competitiveness claim rests on few-shot regimes where fine-tuning is known to be weak.

There is little analysis of *why* souping across heterogeneous SSL objectives works (no weight-distance, loss-landscape, or representational-similarity analysis), so the paper is largely an empirical demonstration rather than an explanatory contribution.

strengths: The paper makes a genuinely new observation: linear mode connectivity can hold between ingredients that differ in their self-supervised training runs (different SSL algorithms and hyperparameters), which is a clear, well-framed extension of the model soup literature.

The experimental design is commendably fair in key places: the 'continued SSL + supervised soup' baseline is given an equal search/development budget (M inter-trainings, N fine-tunings), and comparisons to Model Ratatouille and a SOTA TTA method (SAR) are included. This strengthens the credibility of the modest positive results.
Evaluation breadth is good: 8 ImageNet test sets, 21 VTAB tasks × 16 corruption conditions (336 test sets), and a second stock (Franca ViT-B) to support generality.

Self-Seasoning is a neat, fully unsupervised mixing mechanism, and the few-shot results (Tab. 9, Fig. 4) show a real use case where learned mixture coefficients outperform fine-tuning below ~500 training samples.
The limitations section is honest: the largest gains require unlabeled target/shifted data, other gains are ≤1%, and coverage of SSL algorithms is partial.
weaknesses: The headline gains (+3.5% IN-C, +7% LAION-C) come from inter-training on the shifted/test distribution, which substantially reduces practical novelty: this is essentially offline unsupervised domain adaptation / test-time training relabeled as souping. On-distribution gains are modest (≤1%), and Table 1 shows the Self-Soup uniform mix is sometimes *worse* on IN-Val than baselines. The paper does not clearly enough foreground that the flagship numbers require target-distribution access.

No statistical significance, error bars, or multi-seed evidence is provided for differences of 0.3–0.9% that drive several conclusions (e.g., Self-Soup vs. continued-SSL soup in Tabs. 1, 5, 6, 7). At these effect sizes, single-run comparisons are not convincing.

The central LMC claim is demonstrated only in a very low-compute regime (5-epoch inter-trainings with arbitrary hyperparameters, per §C: 'mostly chosen arbitrarily'). Whether linear mode connectivity holds across SSL algorithms at realistic pretraining scales (hundreds of epochs) is untested, so the 'first to show' claim may not generalize beyond this regime.

Reproducibility is undermined: the 'Data and Code' appendix (§D) contains only the words 'Data.' and 'Code.' with no links or details, despite a GitHub URL in the abstract. Table 7's caption self-referentially says 'the same experiment setup as Tab. 7'; §4.5's fine-tuning learning rates {6e-8, 8e-8, 1e-4, 1.5e-4} appear to contain a typo; and there are assorted typos ('Experments', 'varing').

There is little analysis of *why* mixing works across different SSL objectives (e.g., measuring ingredient diversity, embedding/weight-space distance, or relating to LMC theory). The paper is largely an empirical recipe catalogue; the methodological contribution is thin beyond Eq. (2), which is a straightforward composition of Ratatouille-style inter-training with SSL instead of supervised auxiliary tasks.

The ensemble comparison framing is inconsistent: the paper claims Self-Soups are 'more robust than an ensemble,' yet Table 1 shows the ensemble is best on IN-Val, IN-ReaL, IN-V2, IN-HR, and IN-R, and the Self-Soup ensemble beats the Self-Soup uniform mix nearly everywhere. Selective emphasis weakens the robustness claim.

The TTA comparison (Tab. 3) is somewhat apples-to-oranges: SAR adapts online using only test samples, while the Self-Soup on ImageNet-C was prepared offline with 100K MAE steps on unlabeled shifted data; the resource and data-access assumptions differ and are not normalized.

strengths: Genuinely novel contribution: the paper is the first to show that linear mode connectivity and productive souping can hold between ingredients that differ in their self-supervised training runs (different SSL algorithms, hyperparameters, and data), which meaningfully expands the model-soup literature beyond supervised settings (Figs. 2, 5).

Comprehensive and well-controlled evaluation: eight ImageNet test sets (including ReaL, V2, A, R, C, LAION-C), 21 VTAB tasks across 336 test conditions (clean + 15 corruptions), a second stock (Franca ViT-B), and augmentation-variant ablations (Tabs. 6-7) support the generality of the findings.

Fair and thoughtful baselines: the authors construct a 'continued SSL + supervised soup' baseline with equal search/development cost, include an ensemble comparison (even though it is more expensive at inference), and compare directly against Model Ratatouille (Tab. 5) — showing Self-Soups match it without auxiliary labeled datasets.

The §4.3 experiment is well designed: inter-training on even-indexed test samples and evaluating on odd-indexed samples (disjoint setting) cleanly demonstrates shift-aware robustness gains (+3.5% IN-C, +7% LAION-C) without training on the actual test samples, and comparison against SAR test-time adaptation contextualizes the results.

Self-Seasoning is a sensible unsupervised extension: learning mixture coefficients by minimizing kNN entropy (Eq. 3) is controlled against labeled seasoning using identical ingredients and parameters, and the full PyTorch implementation is provided in the supplement.
Honest limitations discussion (§6) acknowledges that the largest gains require unlabeled shifted data, that other gains are modest, and that only 3 of many SSL families are studied.
weaknesses: Absolute gains are modest outside the corruption settings: on IN-Val, best Self-Soup results (e.g., Uniform Mix 79.09 vs. 79.12 for supervised soup in Tab. 1) are within noise of or slightly below supervised soups, and some cells (e.g., IN-HR Best Ingredient 87.28 vs. 87.34) regress. Headline claims rest mainly on ImageNet-C/LAION-C. No error bars, seeds, or statistical significance tests are reported anywhere, despite many reported differences of <0.3%.

The +7% LAION-C and +3.5% IN-C gains depend on access to unlabeled data from the test/shift distribution, which is a strong practical assumption. The paper does address this honestly and compares to TTA, but the applicability of the largest gains is narrow relative to how prominently they are presented.

Short inter-training runs (5 epochs for the main souping experiment, §4.1) leave open whether LMC across diverse SSL algorithms persists at realistic pre-training scales; the evidence is limited to ViT-B with brief continued training.

Reproducibility gaps in the manuscript itself: the abstract's code URL is truncated ('https://github.com/'), and Section D ('Data and Code') in the supplement is entirely empty. This directly undercuts the paper's reproducibility claim at submission time.

Several typos and inconsistencies undermine polish: 'varing' (§4.5), 'Experments' (Appendix A), self-referential Table 7 caption ('same experiment setup as Tab. 7'), and the fine-tuning learning rates in §4.5 ({6e-8, 8e-8, 1e-4, 1.5e-4}) span an implausible range and appear to contain an error.

Fig. 2 heatmaps are difficult to read (axis labeling of 4 ingredients on 2D axes, and the claim that 'the worst models are always the ingredients alone' is not verifiable from the color scales without more precise reporting); tabulated values for the mixture grid would strengthen the LMC claim.

Section 4.6's claim that 'seasoning can outperform fine-tuning' is supported only for very low sample counts (<500) and only for natural tasks; the fine-tuning baseline dominates elsewhere (Tab. 9), which should be stated more prominently in the main text.
